newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: West tables China rights motion but support fades.
newsitem.headline: West tables China rights motion but support fades.

text.p: The United States and Denmark formally tabled a joint resolution on Thursday to the U.N. Human Rights Commission criticising China's record and seeking reform.

But diplomatic sources said support for the Western-backed motion seemed to be eroding, making it increasingly likely that Beijing escapes censure again for the seventh straight year when the 53-member forum votes next Tuesday.
China was applying diplomatic pressure -- with commercial overtones -- to win backing for its own "no-action motion" which would pre-empt any vote on Denmark's text, they added.
China warned the United States that relations could suffer if it continued to support Denmark's resolution at the U.N. body, which is holding its annual meeting in Geneva.

Australia announced it had struck a deal with China to set up a formal bilateral dialogue on human rights, and revealed it would no longer back the Danish motion. Canada has also edged away from co-sponsoring the text, diplomats said.
No developing country co-sponsored the Danish text -- an indication they are lining up behind Beijing, diplomats said.
A total of 15 states co-sponsored the resolution, including 10 European Union member states, but the United States and Denmark were hoping for more co-sponsors by Tuesday's vote.
"It is a pretty tough game right now for votes..." Tyge Lehmann, head of Denmark's delegation, told Reuters.
"We have 15 countries," Lehmann told reporters, adding that Denmark hoped to have a total of 30 co-sponsors by Tuesday.
"I think some governments are very reluctant to put their name on the resolution, but have promised certainly to support it (when voting)," he said.

Lehmann said it was vital for the credibility of the main U.N. rights forum to at least reject Beijing's no-action motion. The Commission could not afford selectivity, as it is already due to vote on texts condemning abuses in Iraq, Iraq and Burma.
"At least as far as the no-action motion is concerned...it has to do with the credibility of the Commission and its democratic procedures," he said.
"Many governments are keeping their cards close to their chest...What is important is how governments react when it comes to taking action (voting)," he added.

The 15 sponsors are: Austria, Belgium, Britain, Denmark, Finland, Iceland, Ireland, Liechtenstein, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Norway, Portugal, Sweden, Switzerland and the United States. France, Germany, Greece, Italy and Spain were the five EU member states not to co-sponsor.
Lehmann, whose country has been praised by many diplomats for stepping forward to sponsor the resolution after the European Union backed away due to internal discord, added:
"We are really doing our best to defeat the Chinese no-action motion. We know China has been equally active."

Earlier, an American official in Geneva told Reuters: "U.S. officials are optimistic on not losing the no-action motion. We are working energetically to get as many co-sponsors as possible for the Danish resolution.
"We are putting a full-court press on China," the American official added, using a basketball term. "The leaders of the State Department are commited to making this work."

The Danish text expresses concern at "continuing reports of violations of human rights and fundamental freedoms in China by local, provincial and national authorities and severe restrictions on the rights of citizens to the freedoms of assembly, association, expression and religion as well as to due legal process and to a fair trial."
It calls on Beijing to release political prisoners and protect the cultural and ethnic identity of Tibetans and others.
The resolution also calls on China to ratify two major international human rights treaties guaranteeing civil and political freedoms as well as economic and social rights.
A U.S. spokesman told Reuters that if Beijing wanted to improve its bilateral ties, a "good starting point" would be for it to make progress on improving respect for human rights.
